chunks.section: Learning Structured Sparsity for Large Models: Bridging Model Compressibility and Efficient Inference
chunks.text: Tianxiang Xia 1 , Kai Lion 1 , Niao He 1 , Michael Muehlebach 2,3 , Melanie Zeilinger 1 , Hao Ma 4 1 ETH Zürich, Zürich 2 Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, Tübingen 3 Vienna University of Economics and Business, Vienna 4 The University of Hong Kong {xiatia, mzeilinger}@ethz.ch, {kai.lion, niao.he}@inf.ethz.ch, michael.muehlebach@wu.ac.at, haoma@hku.hk † † thanks: Correspondence to: Hao Ma.

Scaling laws continue to reward increases in model scale, while the resulting computational and memory demands drive greater reliance on cloud infrastructure for inference. Yet unreliable network connectivity, communication delays, and privacy requirements can make such reliance impractical, motivating local execution on edge devices. Local deployment requires models to fit within limited memory and execute efficiently with the available computational resources. Recent work has shown that learning sparse-plus-low-rank representations enables elastic compression of a single checkpoint to multiple memory budgets. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into faster inference. Indexing overhead and irregular memory access in unstructured sparse components can offset computational savings. To address this critical deployment barrier, we introduce S-SALAAD, a unified framework that jointly learns the model weights and their low-rank and structured sparse components during training. The framework supports a family of hardware-compatible structured sparsity patterns. It couples this structure learning with budget-aware compression and dedicated CPU and GPU kernels that exploit the learned structure for acceleration, enabling efficient inference from a single checkpoint across memory budgets. Experiments on Llama2 and Qwen3 models, covering both pretraining and distillation, show that S-SALAAD advances the empirical Pareto frontier in perplexity, memory, and inference latency across multiple hardware platforms relative to the evaluated baselines. These results show that structured learning can translate elastic compressibility into reduced memory requirements and lower inference latency, enabling practical deployment of large models on edge devices.

Scaling laws ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ) motivate larger models for improved quality, while their memory and computational demands increase reliance on cloud infrastructure with high-end accelerators. However, network connectivity can be unstable in underwater and rescue operations ( Stojanovic & Preisig, 2009 ; Deng et al., 2013 ; Gunn & Anderson, 2015 ) . Safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving require on-device decisions to avoid cloud communication delays ( Liu et al., 2019 ; Kuutti et al., 2021 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Bodmer et al., 2026 ) , while privacy requirements can prevent sensitive data from being uploaded ( European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2016 ; Shi et al., 2016 ) . These constraints require large-model inference to move from the cloud to resource-constrained edge devices. Fitting large models within limited memory and achieving low inference latency with the available computational resources are the two critical challenges of this transition. The latency requirement is particularly important in feedback control, where inference latency adds to loop delay and excessive delays can degrade closed-loop performance or destabilize the system, compromising safety ( Shin & Cui, 1995 ; Findeisen & Allgöwer, 2004 ; Ma et al., 2026b ; Ma et al., 2023 ; Nan et al., 2026 ) .

To address memory constraints, existing compression methods use quantization ( Dettmers et al., 2022 ) , distillation ( Gu et al., 2024 ) , pruning ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Frantar & Alistarh, 2023 ; Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) , and low-rank factorization ( Hsu et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2025c ) . Varying memory budgets across edge devices call for elastic compression of a single trained checkpoint to multiple model sizes. SALAAD ( Ma et al., 2026a ) enables such elastic compression by learning sparse-and-low-rank (SLR) representations for each linear projection 1 1 1 Here, linear projection refers to a learned linear map in the attention (query/key/value/output) or multi-layer perceptron (MLP; up/gate/down) modules. Embeddings and the language model head are excluded unless noted. during pretraining. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into lower inference latency. Unstructured SLR saves static memory but incurs higher inference latency (see Appendix A.1 ). We identify the overhead from irregular memory access in unstructured sparse operations as a critical barrier to deploying large models on edge devices. Hardware-friendly patterns, including block sparsity ( Okanovic et al., 2025 ) , N : M N\!:\!M sparsity ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , and row-/column-wise sparsity ( Wen et al., 2016 ) , are therefore required to translate these memory savings into efficient edge inference. A straightforward extension of SALAAD is to impose these patterns on its learned sparse components after pretraining. However, our experiments show that this post-hoc conversion can sharply degrade model performance (see Appendix A.2 ). We therefore induce structured sparsity during pretraining , allowing the SLR components to adapt jointly to the structural constraints.

To this end, we introduce S-SALAAD ( S tructured- S parse- A nd- L ow-Rank A daptation via AD MM), a plug-and-play framework that learns structured SLR representations during pretraining for elastic compression and efficient edge inference. Based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), it induces block, N : M N\!:\!M , and row-/column-wise sparsity without changing the model architecture or optimizer update rules. Efficient low-rank updates reduce pretraining overhead, while budget-aware refinement enables zero-shot compression of a single checkpoint to multiple parameter budgets without calibration data or further training. Among these patterns, we identify block sparsity as a practical choice for elastic deployment given current technical capabilities. With dedicated CPU and GPU kernels, the resulting models advance the perplexity–memory–latency Pareto frontier relative to the evaluated baselines. Our contributions are summarized as follows: ❖ A plug-and-play framework for structured-sparsity learning. S-SALAAD jointly learns model weights and their low-rank and structured sparse components under the task loss, adapting the representation to structural constraints during pretraining. S-SALAAD induces block, N : M N\!:\!M , and row-/column-wise sparsity without changing the model architecture, and it is compatible with existing optimizers.

❖ A practical end-to-end implementation. To support the training of larger models and their edge deployment, we address bottlenecks in the training, compression, and inference stages. Specifically, we use i) a warm-started iterative singular value decomposition (I-SVD) to reduce the computational overhead of low-rank updates during pretraining ii) energy-guided alternating refinement (EGAR) to enable zero-shot compression without calibration data or further training, allocating the parameter budget across projections without a preset sparse–low-rank split and reducing reconstruction error within the allocated capacities iii) dedicated CPU and GPU kernels to exploit the induced structured sparsity and reduce inference latency . ❖ Empirical Pareto frontier across training settings. S-SALAAD advances the empirical perplexity–memory–latency Pareto frontier across hardware platforms relative to the evaluated baselines, with each checkpoint supporting multiple compression budgets. These gains hold for Llama2-1B pretraining and cross-architecture distillation from Nemotron-3-Super-120B to Qwen3-1.7B. ❖ Analysis of structured representations. S-SALAAD provides an explicit structured representation of Transformer weights, enabling us to identify distinct sparsity characteristics across linear projection types. Our analysis identifies block sparsity as a practical choice for advancing the perplexity-memory-latency Pareto frontier, combining flexible compression with efficient execution on CPUs and GPUs. Furthermore, we also reveal the relationship between tolerable block granularity and model scale, providing empirical guidance for selecting block sizes when extending S-SALAAD to larger models.

Compression methods for large language models broadly divide into pruning, low-rank factorization, and quantization. Unstructured pruning removes individual weights by magnitude ( Han et al., 2015 ) or calibration-based criteria ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Frantar & Alistarh, 2023 ) , while low-rank methods such as SVD-LLM ( Wang et al., 2025c ) factorize weight matrices and SliceGPT ( Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) shrinks them by removing channels. A second post-hoc family instead runs iterative ADMM on the pretrained weights: ELSA ( Lee et al., 2026 ) pushes unstructured sparsity to extreme ratios, and 3BASiL ( Makni et al., 2025 ) performs layer-wise SLR reconstruction via a 3-block ADMM–both are data-hungry and take hours of GPU-time to compress a single model. Compression-aware pretraining instead induces compressibility during training: LORO ( Mo et al., 2025 ) pretrains in a preset low-rank subspace, SLTrain ( Han et al., 2024 ) augments low-rank pretraining with a fixed-support sparse component, and SALAAD ( Ma et al., 2026a ) jointly learns SLR components via ADMM. The sparse components in SLTrain and SALAAD are unstructured and do not map efficiently onto accelerator primitives. LOST ( Li et al., 2025 ) combines low-rank factors with channel-wise sparsity, but its preset rank and sparse capacity fix the model size during training, and its formulation does not support elastic deployment across budgets from a single checkpoint. It also inserts an additional nonlinearity between the low-rank factors, changing the underlying model architecture. S-SALAAD preserves the original architecture and supports multiple structured sparsity patterns, learning a representation that can be compressed from a single checkpoint to different parameter budgets.

To support large-scale training and elastic edge deployment, we address the computational cost of low-rank updates during pretraining, the zero-shot budget-aware compression of the learned components, and efficient inference on CPUs and GPUs. Training with I-SVD. Algorithm 4.2 summarizes the complete training procedure, which alternates model updates with structured SLR learning. For training efficiency, we update L L , S S , and Y Y once per structured SLR learning phase. Details of the I-Controller are provided in Appendix C.1 . Thus, I-SVD nearly removes the ADMM overhead in S-SALAAD, making end-to-end training practical at scale.

Energy-guided alternating refinement for budget-aware compression. To enable elastic deployment, we need to compress a trained checkpoint to different parameter budgets without calibration data or further training. Among the three supported sparsity patterns, we identify block sparsity as a practical choice for elastic edge deployment, as discussed in Section 5.2 . We therefore develop dedicated CPU and GPU kernels only for block-sparse inference. At inference, the compressed linear map L + S L\!+\!S , with L = A ​ B ⊤ L\!=\!AB^{\top} , is applied to an input activation h ∈ ℝ m h\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{m} as y = ( L + S ) ​ h = ( A ​ B ⊤ + S ) ​ h = A ⁡ ( B ⊤ ​ h ) + S ​ h . y=(L+S)h=(AB^{\top}+S)h=A(B^{\top}h)+Sh. (13)

We first compute y = A ​ B ⊤ ​ h y\!=\!AB^{\top}h using dense kernels, and then accumulate the sparse contribution S ​ h Sh directly into y y , avoiding a separate output buffer for the sparse path. For the sparse path, we store only the retained blocks in a contiguous layout with block-level row pointers and column indices, amortizing indexing overhead across the weights within each block. The kernels skip zero blocks and exploit contiguous access and regular computation within each retained block to reduce inference latency. We implement the GPU kernel in TileLang ( Wang et al., 2025a ) to perform dense tile computations on Tensor Cores, and vectorize the CPU kernel with AVX2. Kernel comparisons are reported in Appendix C.4 .

We pretrain Llama2 models (1B and 350M) on C4 ( Raffel et al., 2020 ) and distill Nemotron-3-Super-120B into Qwen3-1.7B on FineWeb-Edu ( Penedo et al., 2024 ) . Dataset and model details are provided in Appendix D.2 , and training settings in Appendix D.3 . We compare against Wanda ( Sun et al., 2024 ) , SparseGPT ( Frantar & Alistarh, 2023 ) , SliceGPT ( Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) , SVD-LLM ( Wang et al., 2025c ) , LORO ( Mo et al., 2025 ) , vanilla training, and SALAAD ( Ma et al., 2026a ) . We evaluate perplexity, zero-shot downstream accuracy, peak memory, and prefill inference latency. To assess deployment under different memory and compute constraints, we profile inference on Quadro RTX 6000 and RTX 2080 Ti GPUs and 4 × \times AMD EPYC 7662 CPU hosts. Figure 6 compares the perplexity–parameter trade-offs of different block sizes on Llama-350M and Llama-1B, including L L -only (see Appendix B ). Within each model scale, the variants share the same base training configuration, with their settings for structure induction detailed in Appendix D.3 . Retaining S S provides representational flexibility beyond the low-rank component, helping preserve model quality as the parameter budget tightens. Finer blocks impose weaker structural constraints and allow more flexible allocation of sparse capacity during compression. This benefit is evident for the × 8 8\!\times\!8 and × 16 16\!\times\!16 variants on both Llama-350M and Llama-1B at tight budgets (Figures 6(a) and 6(b) ). For example, at 500M parameters on Llama-1B, their perplexities are 17.07 and 17.03, respectively, compared with 17.86 for L L -only.

This representational advantage, however, does not automatically translate into lower inference latency. Dense matrix kernels efficiently support the low-rank path, while fine-grained sparse inference introduces additional overhead. At the 500M operating point on Llama-1B, the × 16 16\!\times\!16 variant achieves lower perplexity but incurs 7.9% higher latency than L L -only at approximately the same peak memory (Figures 6(b) and 4(a) ). Similar overhead is observed on the RTX 2080 Ti and CPU (Figures 23(a) and 24(a) ). Increasing block size trades some compression flexibility for more efficient inference. With × 64 64\!\times\!64 blocks, the perplexity–memory–latency trade-offs closely track those of L L -only on both GPUs (Figures 4(a) and 23(a) ), while improving on them at CPU operating points (Figure 24(a) ). These results demonstrate that an appropriate block granularity enables the sparse component to improve deployment trade-offs beyond the L L -only special case. We note that the block-size benchmark in Appendix C.4 and additional comparisons in Appendix G further characterize this trade-off. The granularity that approximately preserves the L L -only perplexity–parameter trade-off increases from × 16 16\!\times\!16 on Llama-350M to × 64 64\!\times\!64 on Llama-1B (Figure 6 ). This trend suggests that larger models can accommodate coarser, more efficient blocks while retaining elastic compressibility, increasing the deployment benefits of structured S S representations at larger scales.

We presented S-SALAAD, a plug-and-play framework that learns structured SLR representations during training for elastic edge deployment. Zero-shot budget-aware compression and dedicated block-sparse CPU and GPU kernels translate this learned compressibility into memory savings and efficient inference across budgets from a single checkpoint. Across Llama pretraining and Qwen distillation, S-SALAAD advances the empirical perplexity-memory-latency Pareto frontier relative to the evaluated baselines. Our analysis further links tolerable block granularity to model scale, providing empirical guidance for extending the framework to larger models.

chunks.text: We test post-hoc block compression by applying energy-guided alternating refinement (EGAR; Section 4.2 ) to the same SALAAD Llama-1B checkpoint pretrained with unstructured sparsity, under different block constraints and parameter budgets. Table 2 reveals two trends. First, at a fixed budget, perplexity rises as the imposed blocks become coarser. Second, with coarser blocks, perplexity increases more steeply as the parameter budget decreases. These trends are consistent with the reduced pruning flexibility of coarser blocks. Grouping more weights into a single pruning unit restricts which weights can be retained at a given budget, limiting the compressed model’s representational capacity. A checkpoint pretrained with unstructured sparsity has not adapted to these constraints, making post-hoc pruning more damaging as the budget tightens. These results motivate inducing the target structure during pretraining, allowing the sparse and low-rank components to adapt to it under the task loss. This work focuses on reducing the memory footprint and inference latency of large models for edge deployment. Our evaluation uses single-GPU inference on a Quadro RTX 6000 with 24 GB of GPU memory and an RTX 2080 Ti with 11 GB of GPU memory, together with CPU-only inference on 4 × \times AMD EPYC 7662 CPUs with 32 GB of RAM. Edge computing encompasses computation near data sources, including local compute nodes ( Shi et al., 2016 ) . We use these workstation/server platforms as proxies for edge inference in terms of memory capacity and available acceleration, the resource constraints targeted by S-SALAAD. Energy consumption and thermal management are outside the scope of this study.
